top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B011) rests on one precisely stated mechanism: borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on borrowing, so small shocks become large and persistent. The mechanism is nearly thirty years old and has been widely reused, and the credit line is clean because it traces to a single two-author paper. The 2022 overlap concerns banks and bank runs, so it looks like a citation-wording issue and not a disqualifier, provided the citation names only collateral-price feedback and claims no measured effect size. The main weakness is that the channel is identified more indirectly than the firm-level selection margins behind P002. P002 (Helpman and Melitz, B005) is therefore a close second. It is better tested on micro data, but its attribution is harder to draw: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, and Helpman's marginal credit has to be separated from the 2008 prize. P003 (B014) is a serious, well-replicated body of work, but it may combine two achievements under a three-name cap, with Dorn, Acemoglu and Restrepo left out and the China-shock magnitudes still contested. A well-supported award is better than no award, so P000 is last. These assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied committee text, not on independent source verification.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. The profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Hanson or Katz. I am an SSE affiliate alongside committee colleagues Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, which is a collegial tie and not a tie to a candidate. My field is microeconomic theory and market design, which may make me favour a clean mechanism result. This is disclosed, not adjudicated.
